evidence.evidence_gap: Controlled definition and lesson specification ground this prerequisite condition.

hints: Focus on what must remain unchanged between the waves.
Then connect that condition to the positions of maxima and minima.
walkthrough: Coherence is a constant phase difference between two waves.
A constant phase relationship keeps constructive and destructive positions fixed.
Therefore a stable pattern can be observed.

ai_rubric.observable: States that coherence is a constant phase difference between two waves.
Explains that coherence keeps the interference pattern stable or keeps maxima and minima at fixed positions.

hints: Express 7.5 cm as a multiple of 5.0 cm.
Recall the odd half-wavelength condition.
walkthrough: Calculate 7.5/5.0=1.5 wavelengths.
This is an odd half-wavelength path difference, so waves from in-phase sources arrive in antiphase.
Equal amplitudes cancel completely, so select A.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects A: complete destructive interference.

evidence.evidence_gap: This sound-source arrangement is a controlled original application; no mapped leaf directly specifies it.

hints: Look for a common source that fixes the phase relationship.
Also require overlap.
walkthrough: A common signal generator drives both loudspeakers at the same frequency with a fixed phase relationship.
Similar outputs improve the depth of cancellation.
The other arrangements lack coherence, a second source or overlap, so select B.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects B: one signal generator feeding two loudspeakers of similar output.

evidence.evidence_gap: The official leaf supports pattern-condition changes; the amplitude-contrast diagnosis is a controlled original extension.

hints: A deep minimum needs nearly complete cancellation.
Ask what is required for equal opposite displacements.
walkthrough: At a destructive position, opposite displacements cancel most completely when their amplitudes are equal.
Making amplitudes more nearly equal deepens minima while maxima remain strong.
Select A.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects A: make the wave amplitudes at the observation region more nearly equal.

evidence.evidence_gap: This sound-source arrangement is a controlled original application; no mapped leaf directly specifies it.

hints: Use one source to control both loudspeakers.
Describe where the detector moves and what it records.
walkthrough: Treat each part separately.

hints: Name the generator, both sources, overlap and detector.
walkthrough: Connect two loudspeakers to one signal generator so their phase relationship is fixed.
Aim them so their waves overlap.
Move a microphone connected to a level meter through the overlap region and record alternating maxima and minima.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses one signal generator to drive two loudspeakers.
Arranges the sound waves to overlap.
Moves a microphone or suitable detector through the overlap region to record alternating maxima and minima.

hints: Independent oscillators do not normally keep one relative phase.
walkthrough: Independent generators can drift in relative phase, so the sources are not coherent.
The conditions for constructive and destructive interference then change with time.
Maxima and minima move or average out, so the pattern is unstable.

ai_rubric.observable: States that independent generators may have a changing phase difference or are not coherent.
Explains that maxima and minima move or the observed pattern becomes unstable or blurred.

hints: Trace the incident light before it reaches the slits.
Separate source coherence, overlap and observation conditions.
walkthrough: Work from source to screen and keep fringe-spacing calculation outside this lesson.

hints: Both slits receive the same incident wavefront.
walkthrough: The same monochromatic source illuminates both slits.
Each slit therefore emits the same frequency and their phase difference remains constant.
They act as coherent secondary sources.

ai_rubric.observable: States that both slits are illuminated by the same source or wavefront.
States that the emerging waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.

hints: Monochromatic light is already given, so use diffraction, overlap, amplitude balance or detector resolution.
walkthrough: Narrow slits diffract the light so waves spread into the same region.
Close slits help produce usable overlap.
Comparable amplitudes and sufficient screen or detector resolution also improve visibility. State any two distinct valid choices not already supplied in the stem.

ai_rubric.observable: States one valid condition not supplied in the stem, such as narrow slits producing diffraction, sufficient overlap, close slit separation, comparable amplitudes or adequate resolution.
States a second distinct valid condition or design choice not supplied in the stem.

hints: Name both alternating regions.
walkthrough: Constructive interference gives bright regions and destructive interference gives dark regions.
Across the screen these form alternating bright and dark fringes.

ai_rubric.observable: States that alternating bright and dark fringes are observed on the screen.

hints: Subtract the routes before dividing by wavelength.
Connect diffraction at the openings to a wider overlap region.
walkthrough: Carry each result into the next part with its unit or ratio.

hints: Use the magnitude of the route difference.
walkthrough: Calculate Δx=|1.44-1.26|=0.18 m.
Divide by wavelength: 0.18 m / 0.12 m = 1.5.
The path difference is 1.5 wavelengths. Independent check: 1.5×0.12 m=0.18 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the path difference as 0.18 m.
Divides by 0.12 m and obtains 1.5 wavelengths.

hints: Classify 1.5 as a whole or odd half wavelength.
walkthrough: Carry the path difference of 1.5λ.
For in-phase sources, an odd half-wavelength path difference makes the waves arrive in antiphase.
They interfere destructively, so P is an intensity minimum.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies 1.5 wavelengths as an odd half-wavelength path difference that gives antiphase arrival or destructive interference.
Concludes that P is at an intensity minimum.

hints: Recall what an opening does to a wave from Lesson 6.
Connect spreading to the overlap condition.
walkthrough: Diffraction makes the microwaves spread after each opening.
The spreading waves overlap across a wider region.
Where both waves arrive, maxima and minima can be observed.

ai_rubric.observable: States that diffraction makes the microwaves spread after the openings.
Explains that spreading creates a wider overlap region in which maxima and minima can be observed.
